marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q013.takeaway: Nicotinic acid (niacin) lowers triglycerides and LDL/VLDL and can raise HDL, although contemporary lipid therapy decisions require clinical context.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q013.displayText:
Nicotinic acid (niacin) lowers triglycerides and LDL/VLDL and can raise HDL, although contemporary lipid therapy decisions require clinical context.

A man with hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated LDL and VLDL should be treated with a lipid-lowering agent. Thus, the vitamin that can be used to treat this patient is nicotinic acid (niacin or vitamin B3).
Niacin causes a reduction in LDL, VLDL and triglycerides along with increasing HDL. It is the only lipid-lowering agent that lowers lipoprotein (a) levels significantly. The main adverse effect of niacin is cutaneous flushing and pruritus. It can be controlled by pre-treatment with aspirin.
emphasis: Nicotinic acid (niacin) lowers triglycerides and LDL/VLDL and can raise HDL, although contemporary lipid therapy decisions require clinical context

rationales.a: Riboflavin is a flavin coenzyme precursor and is not the vitamin used as a lipid-lowering agent in this item.
rationales.b: Pantothenate contributes to CoA; it is not the vitamin with the lipid effects described.
rationales.d: Pyridoxine is a PLP precursor and does not provide the lipid-lowering effect attributed to nicotinic acid here.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 335; explanation p. 342,343.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q014.takeaway: Niacin reduces adipose lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production, lowering LDL/TAG; it raises rather than lowers HDL.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q014.displayText:
Niacin reduces adipose lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production, lowering LDL/TAG; it raises rather than lowers HDL.

Niacin increases the level of HDL.
Niacin (vitamin B3) is known to inhibit lipolysis within the adipose tissue. Hence, the circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) are reduced. The liver normally uses these circulating FFAs as a precursor in the synthesis of triacylglycerol (TAG). As a result, niacin causes a reduction in liver TAG synthesis. TAGs are in turn required for very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) and low density lipoprotein (LDL) synthesis. Therefore both plasma VLDL and LDL values are reduced. Overall, niacin decreases LDL, VLDL and TAG levels, and increases high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels. Thus it is particularly useful in the treatment of type IIb hyperlipoproteinemia, in which both VLDL and LDL are elevated.
emphasis: Niacin reduces adipose lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production, lowering LDL/TAG; it raises rather than lowers HDL

rationales.a: Niacin inhibits adipose lipolysis, reducing circulating free fatty acids; this statement is true.
rationales.b: Reduced fatty-acid delivery to liver lowers TAG synthesis and VLDL secretion; this statement is true.
rationales.d: Niacin can lower LDL as part of its lipid effects; the false statement is that it lowers HDL.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 335; explanation p. 343.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q015.takeaway: Pantothenic acid is part of coenzyme A, which transfers acyl groups in pathways including fatty-acid oxidation and the TCA cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q015.displayText:
Pantothenic acid is part of coenzyme A, which transfers acyl groups in pathways including fatty-acid oxidation and the TCA cycle.

Pantothenic acid constitutes a part of the coenzyme A.
The primary function of coenzyme A (pantothenic acid) is to transfer acyl groups. Pantothenic acid as coenzyme A is involved in:
Fatty acid oxidation
TCA cycle (as succinyl Co-A and acetyl Co-A)
Cholesterol synthesis (as HMG Co-A)
Acetylation reactions
emphasis: Pantothenic acid is part of coenzyme A, which transfers acyl groups in pathways including fatty-acid oxidation and the TCA cycle

rationales.a: Thiamine is the precursor of TPP, not the vitamin component of CoA.
rationales.b: Riboflavin gives rise to FMN and FAD; it is not the CoA vitamin component.
rationales.d: Pyridoxine gives rise to PLP, used in amino-acid metabolism, rather than CoA.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 336; explanation p. 343.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q016.takeaway: Pantothenic acid (B₅) contains β-alanine and deficiency is classically associated with burning-feet syndrome.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q016.displayText:
Pantothenic acid (B₅) contains β-alanine and deficiency is classically associated with burning-feet syndrome.

The vitamin that is deficient in burning feet syndrome is vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) which contains the amino acid beta-alanine.
Pantothenic acid deficiency is rarely seen as the vitamin is abundantly found in food (egg yolks, whole grains, vegetables). Burning feet syndrome is classically seen in pantothenic acid deficiency. The other symptoms of pantothenic deficiency are non-specific and include GI disturbances, paraesthesia, muscle cramps and ataxia.
Beta-alanine is an amino acid seen in:
Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
Coenzyme A
Carnosine
Anserine
Acyl carrier protein
emphasis: Pantothenic acid (B₅) contains β-alanine and deficiency is classically associated with burning-feet syndrome

rationales.a: Phenylalanine is not the amino-acid component of pantothenate; the relevant moiety is β-alanine.
rationales.b: Arginine is not incorporated as the amino-acid component of pantothenic acid.
rationales.d: Tryptophan is a precursor for niacin synthesis, whereas pantothenic acid contains β-alanine.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 336; explanation p. 343,344.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q017.takeaway: Biotin carries activated CO₂ in carboxylase reactions, including pyruvate and acetyl-CoA carboxylation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q017.displayText:
Biotin carries activated CO₂ in carboxylase reactions, including pyruvate and acetyl-CoA carboxylation.

Biotin serves as an important cofactor in carboxylation reactions
Biotin (vitamin B7) functions as a carrier for the activated carbon dioxide molecule in carboxylation reactions. The enzymes using biotin as a cofactor are acetyl CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl CoA carboxylase and methyl crotonyl CoA carboxylase.
Malic enzyme and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and II do not use biotin as a coenzyme. Gamma carboxylation by vitamin K is also biotin-independent.
emphasis: Biotin carries activated CO₂ in carboxylase reactions, including pyruvate and acetyl-CoA carboxylation

rationales.a: Thiamine supports decarboxylation and carbon transfer reactions, but it is not the cofactor that carries CO₂ in carboxylation.
rationales.b: Riboflavin supplies redox cofactors FMN/FAD, not the covalently bound CO₂ carrier for carboxylases.
rationales.c: Pyridoxine yields PLP for amino-acid reactions; biotin is the required carboxylase cofactor.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 336; explanation p. 344.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q018.takeaway: Raw egg white avidin binds dietary biotin; deficiency can impair pyruvate carboxylase and cause exercise intolerance.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q018.displayText:
Raw egg white avidin binds dietary biotin; deficiency can impair pyruvate carboxylase and cause exercise intolerance.

The patient developed pyruvate carboxylase enzyme deficiency.
Individuals who eat an excess of uncooked egg-white develop biotin deficiency and as a result carboxylase enzyme deficiency. This is because a protein called avidin present in the egg-white binds to biotin in the diet and makes biotin unavailable for intestinal absorption. Biotin deficiency can cause dermatitis, mental status changes (depression, hallucinations), paraesthesia and alopecia.
Biotin serves as a co-enzyme for the synthesis of several carboxylase enzymes such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl CoA carboxylase and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase. Thus these enzymes are deficient in biotin deficiency.
emphasis: Raw egg white avidin binds dietary biotin; deficiency can impair pyruvate carboxylase and cause exercise intolerance

rationales.a: Glucose-6-phosphatase is not biotin dependent; it releases glucose-6-phosphate-derived glucose in liver and kidney.
rationales.b: Glycogen phosphorylase uses PLP rather than biotin, so egg-white-associated biotin deficiency does not target it directly.
rationales.d: PEP carboxykinase uses GTP in gluconeogenesis and is not a biotin-dependent carboxylase.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 336; explanation p. 344.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q019.takeaway: Humans obtain vitamin B₁₂ primarily from animal-derived foods because only microorganisms synthesize cobalamin.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q019.displayText:
Humans obtain vitamin B₁₂ primarily from animal-derived foods because only microorganisms synthesize cobalamin.

Vitamin B12 is found maximum in animal products.
Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is synthesized only by microorganisms. Thus, the only source of cobalamin for humans is animal products. It is not found in plant sources. Therefore, individuals who are strict vegetarians are usually at the risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency.
emphasis: Humans obtain vitamin B₁₂ primarily from animal-derived foods because only microorganisms synthesize cobalamin

rationales.b: Green leafy vegetables provide folate and other nutrients but are not a reliable natural source of cobalamin.
rationales.c: Roots and tubers are plant foods and do not supply the human dietary B₁₂ source identified here.
rationales.d: An unfortified vegetarian diet lacks the usual animal-derived cobalamin sources, which is why strict vegetarians are at risk.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 337; explanation p. 344.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q020.takeaway: High-dose niacin infusion can cause macular edema and cysts, in addition to flushing, hepatotoxicity and glucose intolerance.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH21_Q020.displayText:
High-dose niacin infusion can cause macular edema and cysts, in addition to flushing, hepatotoxicity and glucose intolerance.

Macular cysts and edema may develop in patients due to the infusion of supraphysiological doses of vitamin B3 (niacin toxicity).
The toxic effects of niacin include:
Flushing associated with skin dryness, itching, paresthesia, and headache is seen. These effects may be seen with even a low dose of 30mg/day. Pre-medication with aspirin alleviates these symptoms as these symptoms are mediated by prostaglandins.
Macular edema and macular cysts
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
Hepatic toxicity presents as jaundice with elevated AST and ALT levels.
Fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation.
Glucose intolerance
Hyperuricemia
emphasis: High-dose niacin infusion can cause macular edema and cysts, in addition to flushing, hepatotoxicity and glucose intolerance

rationales.a: Vitamin A toxicity is associated with intracranial hypertension, skin changes and liver effects, not this niacin infusion-related maculopathy.
rationales.b: Vitamin D toxicity primarily causes hypercalcemia and soft-tissue calcification rather than niacin-associated macular edema.
rationales.c: Vitamin E is an antioxidant; the dose-related macular cysts described are linked to niacin.
